Why isn't "shutdown now" the default behavior of shutdown?

Shutdown is a command and now is a parameter. It's like anything else you run.

When you run "ls" you can't just type "ls" you have to tell it where you want it to run and you can then make it do other things.

You first invoke "shutdown", they you have to tell "shutdown" what you want it to do.

I understand parameters. A time frame should be an option in my opinion. If I simply tell the operating system to shut down, it shouldn't have to schedule it for some time in the near future, it should just shut down.

Also, it will notify the users even with "now"; "system is going down for reboot NOW", I think is the text you get when rebooting.

Because normally you don't just shutdown without warning users. Fun fact, shutdown used to power off at least Solaris. No shutdown, no passing init. POOF.

Now though it's a mess. Shutdown, halt, poweroff, they can all do different, unpredictable things. I mean, this is just retarded:

$ file /usr/sbin/{poweroff,halt,shutdown}
/usr/sbin/poweroff: symbolic link to `../bin/systemctl'
/usr/sbin/halt: symbolic link to `../bin/systemctl'
/usr/sbin/shutdown: symbolic link to `../bin/systemctl'
$
$ file /usr/sbin/{poweroff,halt,shutdown} -L
/usr/sbin/poweroff: ELF 64-bit LSB shared object, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked (uses shared libs), for GNU/Linux 2.6.32, BuildID[sha1]=f220bd2899cb6c11ec283b90cc5364e4be0c1b2e, stripped
/usr/sbin/halt: ELF 64-bit LSB shared object, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked (uses shared libs), for GNU/Linux 2.6.32, BuildID[sha1]=f220bd2899cb6c11ec283b90cc5364e4be0c1b2e, stripped
/usr/sbin/shutdown: ELF 64-bit LSB shared object, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked (uses shared libs), for GNU/Linux 2.6.32, BuildID[sha1]=f220bd2899cb6c11ec283b90cc5364e4be0c1b2e, stripped
$

And halting a modern PC is hardly what you want to do these days. It should close the OS and get the computer into the step before turning off without actually turning off. It will sit there in some power state with some things running waiting for a hardware poweroff or reset. I guess it might immediately jump there on some systems (like Solaris you mentioned).

Difference is control. Especially in the case of an emergency (power failure fe), or IO problems, I want the ability to enter all of those states, on my own terms. By linking to a binary file like systemdickhead does I can't tell what exactly it's doing. I know there are a few cases where it will timeout and finish the reboot on its own. Not fun when you have a database still coming down. I don't think I can even cancel a shutdown any more.

Given PC's don't really have a BOS or firmware preboot any more, "halted" kinda lost meaning. Kinda surprised someone hasn't done it with grub. Why can't the OS call grub again on shutdown instead of rebooting, beats going through a full post again and could load vnc or something in grub. Serial consoles are still quite handy in a pinch.

If I don't specify a timeframe as an option, I believe the default behavior should be to do what I told it immediately. I don't have to tell any other program (that I'm aware of) when to execute if I want it done immediately.

I agree with you that the behavior of shutdown deviates from 'typical' but I prefer this.

It's a nice fail safe from accidentally hitting the wrong command in history, brain farts, etc.
